newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss prosecutor warns of mafia investor threat.
newsitem.headline: Swiss prosecutor warns of mafia investor threat.

text.p: Switzerland's top prosecutor on Wednesday warned that foreign crime gangs could buy their way into big Swiss companies as a way of hiding huge illegal profits from the law.

Federal Prosecutor Carla del Ponte told bankers and lawyers that organised crime could import violence and corruption into quiet Switzerland in its quest to launder money -- find a legitimate disguise for dirty money.

"Switzerland is especially affected by the issue of money laundering as a great deal of money is sent here because we are a good financial centre, and of course some of it is dirty money," del Ponte told a conference of financial experts.
"Right now we only have the money but in a short time the owners could come here and then things will look different," she said.

Switzerland made money laundering a crime in 1990 and loosened its tight banking secrecy laws after worldwide pressure to erect barriers against a growing international flow of criminal profits, especially from narcotics.

Del Ponte said money laundering remained a problem in Switzerland and elsewhere, especially in so-called offshore financial centres, countries with weak regulations where Swiss and other world banks have branch offices.
The prosecutor said there were already a few cases where crime gangs had invested cash in small Swiss companies as a way of turning dirty profits into legally clean assets.
"When they have a stake, then they want to have a say in the business," she said about mafia-style gangs, which investigators have said come mainly from Italy, Eastern Europe and Latin America.

"Switzerland is a quiet country and you can go about without being in danger, as you would be in other countries. But when they (gangs) come with shares or a stake in a company, they bring an element of violent crime," she said.
Asked whether organised crime stakes could spread to big, publicly-traded Swiss companies, she said: "No, so far only in privately-held companies. What I am saying is, be careful."
